Mounjaro and Zepbound are the same drug. Both contain tirzepatide, both are made by Eli Lilly, and both are once-weekly injections.

The difference is the label. Mounjaro was approved first, for type 2 diabetes. Zepbound is the name Lilly uses in the United States for weight management. Same molecule, two brand names, two sets of approved uses.

In Indonesia, only Mounjaro is registered. BPOM approved it for type 2 diabetes in February 2026 and added weight management in July 2026, so here one brand covers both uses.

What are Mounjaro and Zepbound?

Mounjaro is Eli Lilly’s brand of tirzepatide that was first approved for type 2 diabetes. Outside the United States, including in Indonesia, it is also approved for weight management.

Zepbound is Lilly’s US brand of tirzepatide for weight management. In the US, it is also approved for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with obesity.

Both brands contain the same active ingredient, tirzepatide, and nothing else as the active drug. If you want the science behind it, we walk through how tirzepatide works in a separate guide.

In short, tirzepatide is a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, sometimes called a “twincretin”. It copies two gut hormones that raise insulin when blood sugar is high and help you feel full sooner. When the FDA approved Mounjaro in May 2022, Lilly described it as the first approved medicine to act on both receptors.

Because the molecule is the same, the dose steps are the same too. Both brands come in six strengths: 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5 and 15 mg, taken once a week.

Online, tirzepatide is sometimes called “tirz” or “GLP-2 TRZ”. These are shorthand names, not brands, and they do not mean Mounjaro or Zepbound.

What each brand is approved for

The only real difference between the two brands is what each label covers, and where. In the United States, Lilly split tirzepatide into two brands. The European Union, the UK and Indonesia use the Mounjaro name for both diabetes and weight management.

Mounjaro Zepbound
Active ingredient Tirzepatide Tirzepatide
Maker Eli Lilly Eli Lilly
US approved uses Type 2 diabetes (May 2022) Chronic weight management (November 2023); moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with obesity (December 2024)
European Union and UK Type 2 diabetes and weight management Not used
Indonesia (BPOM) Type 2 diabetes (February 2026) and weight management (July 2026) Not registered

So when someone outside the US says they are “on Mounjaro for weight loss”, they are using the same medicine an American would get as Zepbound. The label differs; the drug inside the pen does not.

Pens and vials: how the formats differ

The second visible difference is the device. Over the past few years, Lilly has sold tirzepatide in three formats:

  • Single-dose pen. The original US Mounjaro and Zepbound pens hold one weekly dose, with a hidden needle that is already attached.
  • Single-dose vial. In August 2024, Lilly started selling Zepbound in vials for self-paying US patients through LillyDirect, first at 2.5 mg and 5 mg. Patients draw each dose with a syringe. By mid-2025, Lilly said all six strengths would come in vials.
  • KwikPen. This multi-dose pen holds four weekly doses, a month of treatment in one device. The UK regulator approved the four-dose Mounjaro KwikPen in January 2024. In February 2026, Lilly launched a Zepbound KwikPen in the US.

The format changes how you inject, not what you inject. A 5 mg dose from a KwikPen, a single-dose pen or a vial is the same 5 mg of tirzepatide. If you are given a pen type you have not used before, ask your pharmacist to show you how it works, since the steps differ between devices.

Where each brand is sold, and what that means in Indonesia

Zepbound is a US brand. Mounjaro is the name Lilly uses in the European Union, the UK, Indonesia and other markets.

Here, Mounjaro was launched in Jakarta on 4 July 2026, with Indonesia’s Vice Minister of Health introducing it as a new prescription medicine. BPOM’s approval covers both type 2 diabetes and weight management, so Indonesian patients do not need a second brand for weight loss.

That has two practical consequences:

  • If you see Zepbound offered for sale in Indonesia, it is not a product registered with BPOM. The molecule may be the same, but nobody in Indonesia has checked that particular pack.
  • If your doctor abroad prescribed Zepbound, the brand with the same molecule here is Mounjaro. A doctor in Indonesia needs to prescribe it and decides the strength. The pen may look different, so check how to use it before your first dose.

Either way, a genuine Mounjaro pack sold in Indonesia carries a BPOM registration number that you can look up on cekbpom.pom.go.id.

Can you switch between Mounjaro and Zepbound?

Switching between them changes the brand, not the medicine. In the US, the brand a doctor prescribes usually follows the diagnosis, since each label lists different uses.

A few points still matter:

  • Never use both at once. Two tirzepatide brands together means a double dose of the same drug.
  • Let your doctor set the strength. The strengths match across brands, but your doctor decides which one you continue on.
  • Learn the new device. A KwikPen, a single-dose pen and a vial with a syringe each work differently.

If you are moving to Indonesia or staying here for a while, the same logic applies to Zepbound and Mounjaro. You are continuing tirzepatide under its local name.

How the tirzepatide brands compare with the semaglutide brands

Novo Nordisk did the same thing with semaglutide. Ozempic is the diabetes brand and Wegovy is the weight-management brand, and both contain semaglutide. Mounjaro and Zepbound are Lilly’s version of that split.

Indonesia handles the two molecules differently. Semaglutide has two registered brands here, Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for weight management. Tirzepatide has one, Mounjaro, which carries both uses.

For most readers, the bigger question is tirzepatide versus semaglutide: two different molecules with different actions. We look at that in our comparison of tirzepatide vs semaglutide.

Conclusion

Mounjaro and Zepbound are the same medicine. Both contain tirzepatide, both come from Eli Lilly, and both use the same six weekly strengths. What separates them is the label: Mounjaro started as the diabetes brand, and Zepbound is the US brand for weight management and sleep apnoea.

In Indonesia, the choice is simpler. Only Mounjaro is registered, and since July 2026 it covers both type 2 diabetes and weight management. If you were prescribed Zepbound abroad, talk to a doctor here about continuing tirzepatide as Mounjaro, and check the BPOM number on the pack you receive.

Frequently asked questions

Is Zepbound the same as Mounjaro?

Yes, in what it contains. Both are tirzepatide from Eli Lilly, in the same six strengths. They differ in approved uses and in the markets where each name is sold.

Is Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro?

No. The strengths are identical, from 2.5 mg to 15 mg once a week. A 10 mg dose of Zepbound is the same as a 10 mg dose of Mounjaro.

Is Zepbound available in Indonesia?

No. Zepbound is not registered with BPOM. In Indonesia, tirzepatide is sold as Mounjaro, which is approved for both type 2 diabetes and weight management.

Can Mounjaro be used for weight loss in Indonesia?

Yes. BPOM added weight management to Mounjaro’s approval in July 2026. It needs a doctor’s prescription.

Why does Zepbound exist if Mounjaro is the same drug?

In the United States, Lilly gave tirzepatide a separate brand name when the FDA approved it for weight management in November 2023. Mounjaro kept its type 2 diabetes label.

Is Zepbound approved for sleep apnoea?

In the United States, yes. In December 2024, the FDA approved Zepbound for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with obesity.
